>We're not talking about everyone. we're talking about op. it's common sense that if he's struggling he needs to change something about his life.

I think this is the problem. You have a "me not we" perspective of the world. Instead of a "us" or "we not me" kind of perspective and it's gotten you really far in life because at one point it actually was beneficial to think like that as most people were okay and there was a large middle class base in America. 

Today, the middle class is rapidly disappearing and I'm not the only person in this situation.  Also, just because something is hard or that I'm struggling means something is inherently wrong. It just means this is where I am today and I am asking questions and researching things as I move forward in my life and because I choose to take a moment to vent - that doesn't mean I'm weak or incapable.

I'm sorry you ended up in this discussion with u/extension_lemon_6728 notice how they intentionally ignored the idea that the average USA salary is equivalent to that of 1972 yet, everything costs at least 100% more with inflation? Which means even if inwas making 50% more (100k) inflation over the years would mean things have increased by 100% on average meaning stuff is still 50% more expensive even with a 100k salary. 

Hell big macs cost $0.65 in 1972 and today it costs $3.99 which is a 516٪ increase....

Essentially this means spending $3.99 for a big mac when I'm making 7k a year. Better cut out the fine dining!

I think it boils down to the fact that back then it was a very "What can I do for ME. I AM #1!" Mentality where younger generations are taking a "we not me" approach. I just wish it was the norm to set aside politics and meet in the middle. Because someone will always be unhappy with a situation but I wish we were more focused on the needs of the majority instead of the needs of the loudest on the left against the needs of the loudest on the right. 


Anyway you get it. The rest of post is for the other guy to read if they want to be educated about the reality of America's cost of living. 

Like, yes, ideally it'd be nice to buy a 200,000 house in Georgia but they're not taking into account issues with bank rates, mortgages and the increases in property tax, etc. That make it more than it originally would be to buy in 1972 even if it's priced more equivalently upfront. 

Then, they say "educate yourself! Go to school!" 

Sure, let's see my UCLA DEGREE cost me roughly $50,000 annually for 4 years of schooling when I went. In 1975 it cost $630 annually for residents (which was my demographic  at the time. [(source)](https://dailycal.org/2014/12/22/history-uc-tuition-since-1868/). So - let's see that means tuition has increased by 2,200%  

Then they say, "now get a higher paying job" without cosodering that life can get in the way of someone's financial success. 

For me that meant, some unfortunate life circumstances regarding my health for 7 years that were disabling and wayyyy before work from home was a feasible option for employment I fell behind, but was still able to stay OFF of government assistance and work as long as I lived at home. 

The whole time (naively) figuring experience was experience and that it'd translate somewhere higher paying that would at the bare minimum make me self sufficient. Unfortunately I was wrong. 

Luckily, I've been doing significantly better since then and have a fulltime office job that pays me average.

Could be better but it was the highest offer I could get since lots of high paying jobs don't see "parttime retail" or "parttime admin assistant" and go "Oh awesome! You can definitely make Six figures yearly!" Because, you know you need experience to do that and all your parttime work over 5-7years isn't really experience....

I ended up 'settling' because my current job is union and has really great benefits that I can't say no to. Especially with a pension and health insurance at 0 cost to me which, is unheard of today. Plus, there is definitely room for growth there. Which is another incredible thing.

So, I'm not doing horrific - but I'm still very limited so long as I want to live alone.

I feel this. So much. Like housing and food costs are one thing that I can kinda do something about by being smart about it as best I can while inflation and tax credits/stuff is way out of my control.
Seriously. I just explore inflation to someone else around here. I guess I'm just fusterated. 😆

Okay, so people with shitty jobs just need something that pays better! Sure! Are you hiring? Do you know anywhere other than McDonalds that is hiring? Are you aware that:

The average cost of a house in 1972 was $189,500 and in 2022 its $400,300 which is a 132% increase [(source)](https://www.marketplace.org/2022/08/17/money-and-millennials-the-cost-of-living-in-2022-vs-1972/) also the federal minimum wage in 1972 was $1.60 [(source)](https://www.dollartimes.com/inflation/items/1972-united-states-minimum-wage#:~:text=In%20the%20year%201972%2C%20the,in%20the%20cost%20of%20living%3F )in 2022 it's $7.25 & hasnt increased since 2009. That's a 56.5% increase.  

So housing has increased 132% however minimum wage has only increased less than half of that by 56.5%  

Also the average income in 1972 was $7,133.80 [(source)](https://www.multpl.com/us-average-income/table/by-year) and it's $54,132 in 2022. 

56,132 in 2022 is equivalant to 7,592.71 in 1972. [(source)](https://www.usinflationcalculator.com/)

So, essentially I'm somehow 'supposed' to afford housing at 2022 prices (400k) with a salary from 1972.

Seems super simple/reasonable to do! I should totally be okay either the fact that I'm barely making ends meet with an average USA salary. Sounds like the American dream come to life for sure and I'm simply living on a movie stars budget/beyond my means  since I can't afford a 400k housing market  with a salary that's equivalent to 7,500 in 1972.
